claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a finely interwoven, multiphase microstructure.
Its heterogeneous phase boundaries support the formation of nascent protective oxide or spinel layers at elevated temperature.
A protective oxide layer formed at elevated temperature can increase the wear resistance of a multiphase HEA.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes protective oxide or spinel films at eutectic phase boundaries.
Removal of the boundary oxide exposes microscale sites susceptible to localized galvanic corrosion.
Electrochemical potential differences among the constituent phases drive localized galvanic corrosion.
Localized corrosion impedes protective-film reformation or further destabilizes the film.
Reciprocal film removal and localized corrosion form a positive feedback loop.
The proposed feedback loop synergistically accelerates both wear and corrosion.
Annealing or homogenization can reduce the density or vulnerability of interphase boundaries.
The proposed microstructural modification can be made while keeping overall composition and bulk properties constant.
The unmodified-boundary alloy will have a higher total degradation rate than the stated baseline sample.
Vulnerable unmodified boundaries will produce a higher wear rate because protective layers are removed more frequently.
Vulnerable unmodified boundaries will produce a higher corrosion rate because of localized galvanic attack.
Samples with strengthened or homogenized interphase boundaries will show lower total degradation under identical conditions.
Homogenized samples will show lower individual wear and corrosion rates than as-cast samples.
The exact quantitative degradation changes depend on microstructural characteristics and processing parameters.
A controlled comparison will use as-cast and homogenized samples under identical simultaneous sliding-wear and corrosive conditions at approximately 700 degrees Celsius.
Total degradation, wear rate, corrosion rate, oxide integrity, and localized corrosion features are measurable comparison outcomes.
Failure of the homogenized samples to show a statistically significant reduction in total degradation and in both individual wear and corrosion rates is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says the alloy with unmodified boundaries has higher degradation relative to the baseline, but the baseline and experimental control are themselves described as as-cast samples with unmodified, fine interphase boundaries. Thus the stated higher-degradation specimen is not clearly distinct from its baseline.

The intervention requires microstructural modification while keeping bulk properties constant, whereas the experimental design specifies homogenizing annealing without a control or verification that phase fractions, hardness, strength, or other wear-relevant bulk properties remain constant.
